paper_title: WMIP: A Working-Memory-Inspired Programmable Probe of Cumulative State Tracking in Large Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Human working memory lets people maintain and update information. Large language models (LLMs) face a related demand when tracking updates within a single prompt without writing out intermediate states, yet existing tests differ in their constraints on written steps. We introduce a working-memory-inspired probe of cumulative state tracking with program-computed answers, 3 to 100 updates, and final-state, intermediate-state, or multi-target queries. It compares protocols on identical items. Across 18 LLMs, accuracy is 84.9% on single-step arithmetic but 31.7% on core items requiring one number after three to seven updates. From 50 updates on, no model exceeds 10% accuracy. Core accuracy reaches 88.0% under a larger budget and instructions to write steps and place the answer on the last line, mainly due to the instruction changes rather than the budget. Core accuracy also correlates positively with public Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard scores. These findings show that strong single-step arithmetic does not ensure reliable cumulative tracking and that output protocols substantially change measured accuracy. We release the generator, items, scoring code, and responses for reproducible comparisons across depths, query types, and protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Keeping running score in ones head relies on working memory, which holds information briefly and updates it as changes arrive (Baddeley and Hitch, 1974; Miyake et al., 2000). Large language models (LLMs) meet similar demand when prompt lists an initial state and series of updates and asks for the result without written steps (cf. Nye et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2022). Such state tracking underlies many uses of LLMs, from understanding narratives and instructions to stateful, multi-turn tool use (Kim and Schuster, 2023; Patil et al., 2025). Much as people write down information they need to remember (Risko and Gilbert, 1 2016), models written steps record intermediate states, which removes this demand (Nye et al., 2021). Testing this demand therefore requires controlling how prompt wording (Mizrahi et al., 2024), output budgets, and scoring rules constrain written steps. Existing state-tracking tests share this structure but constrain written steps differently. Minerva, for example, allows 4,096 output tokens, so models can write out the operations (Xia et al., 2025). These tests may therefore not all pose this demand. We present working-memory-inspired probe of cumulative state tracking (Figure 1). Its generator sets the number of updates, and its protocols set how much room is left for written steps. Under the core protocol, 16-token budget and the oneinteger rule leave little room for written steps. Without written steps, all 18 models answer the core items less accurately than single-step arithmetic, and accuracy falls as sequences grow. Asking for written steps (Kojima et al., 2022) raises core accuracy from 31.7% to 88.0%, so protocol choices change what is measured. Core accuracy also correlates positively with public Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) scores (Patil et al., 2025) (Section 4.6). We make three contributions. generator with adjustable depth, executable answers, and final-state, intermediate-state, and multi-target queries, released with items, code, and responses. Same-item comparisons showing substantial protocol effects on measured accuracy, with sensitivity analyses across wordings, seeds, and depths. Positive BFCL associations across 18 models, compared with those of single-step arithmetic and cancellation controls. Figure 1: In working-memory-inspired probe, LLM accuracy falls as updates accumulate when models answer without written steps. (a) The probe mirrors human working-memory updating tasks (Miyake et al., 2000), in which an update can transform held value rather than only replace it (Ecker et al., 2010). The core protocol restricts written steps, paralleling participants need to keep values in mind, but keeps the full update sequence visible. In the abridged example (full prompt in Section 3.1), Claude Haiku 4.5 answers incorrectly under the core protocol and correctly under the written-steps protocol. (b) Accuracy pooled over the 18 models. Solid lines compare protocols on the 60 core items (K = 3, 5, 7). The dashed line extends the core protocol to depth items (K 10) from the same generator. The diamond marks single-step arithmetic on separate items.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Entity tracking moves objects among boxes (Kim and Schuster, 2023), and BIG-Bench Hard tracks pairwise object swaps with multiple-choice answers (Suzgun et al., 2023). Our core instead applies integer updates to three named entities and requests one free-response integer. Minervas quantity-state task is closest in content but allows 4,096 output tokens, enough to work through updates in writing (Xia et al., 2025). GSM-Infinite varies operation counts but requests step-by-step reasoning (Zhou et al., 2025). Our core allows 16 tokens and scores exactly one integer. Writtensteps and large-budget protocols relax these limits on the same items. LLM working-memory studies use match detection on n-back tasks (Gong et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), and tested models meet or exceed human norms on span tasks (de Langis et al., 2026). Wang and Sun (2026) ask for the last value of repeatedly overwritten key. Unlike human operation span (Conway et al., 2005), our probe keeps every initial value and update visible. Working memory therefore motivates the demand tested here, without establishing equivalence to human span tasks. Representation probes and interventions can distinguish state-tracking algorithms (Li et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026), but final answers cannot show whether models maintain or recompute states. Benchmark scores depend on paraphrased instructions and task-preserving formatting (Mizrahi et al., 2024; Sclar et al., 2024). Output-format restrictions can affect reasoning accuracy (Tam et al., 2024). Motivated by measurement-validity recommendations (Bean et al., 2025), we report integer compliance, truncation, and seed and wording sensitivity alongside accuracy. BFCL evaluates function calling, including stateful, multi-step interactions (Patil et al., 2025), and shares no items with the probe. Comparing the cores BFCL association with those of simpler controls follows discriminant-validation logic (Campbell and Fiske, 1959). Appendix provides additional task and methodological comparisons.

sections.title: 3.1 Generating state-tracking tasks
sections.content: Core items initialize three named entities with integers, list ordered gains, losses, or transfers between them, and query one entitys final value (Figure 2). Initial values range from 5 to 20, gains from 1 to 10, losses from 1 to 5, and transfers from 1 to 3. The reference answer is the queried entitys initial value plus its signed changes, so update order does not change it. short program computes it and counts the updates to that entity (median 2 at = 3 and 45.5 at = 100). fixed redraw rule excludes core and depth items where that entity is never updated or finishes at its initial value, preventing correct answers from copying the initial value. Each item is one user message. Although the prompt says the initial state cannot be consulted again, the full sequence remains in context. The 2 Figure 2: Probe workflow. (1) Code generates items and computes reference answers. (2) Four response protocols are applied to the same core items. (3) Responses are scored and truncation is flagged. (4) Performance is compared across conditions and related to BFCL scores. The response 28 is Claude Haiku 4.5s recorded response (Figure 1a). The other two illustrate the scoring rules. core prompt ends with Respond with ONLY the final number. and allows 16 output tokens. One complete core prompt reads as follows. You will track sequence of point updates. You cannot refer back to the initial state after reading it once. Initial state: Leo: 15 points, James: 18 points, Carol: 15 points Operations (apply in order): 1. Carol gives 2 points to Leo. 2. Leo loses 2 points. 3. Leo loses 3 points. After all operations, how many points does Leo have? Respond with ONLY the final number. The reference answer is 12. Appendix details task generation and prompt variants.

sections.title: 3.3 Response scoring
sections.content: Core, depth, arithmetic, cancellation, wording, instruction-variant, and intermediate-state responses require exactly one extracted integer matching the executable answer (one-integer rule, Figure 2). Zero or multiple integers receive zero credit. Written steps uses the last integer (lastinteger rule). Large budget uses both rules. Multitarget responses must give exactly integers matching the reference values in the requested order (Appendix G). The parser removes dollar signs and supported thousands separators before extraction but allows surrounding prose, so compliance differs from bare-number answer. We report correct, one-integer-wrong, and noncompliant responses. Truncation, the services length finish reason, can overlap any outcome. All core items remain in the denominator. Assignment and set and count items use two parsers, reported in parallel with no primary parser. Parser 2 requires one distinct correct vocabulary member for assignment, and one correct integer or exact set equality for sets and counts. Parser 1 permits more substring, numerical-position, and empty-set matches. Appendix specifies both parsers and their seven differing labels. All 18 models answered all 840 main-bank requests, with no missing responses. Ten ran locally and eight through APIs (Appendix C, scores in Table 2). GPT-5.2 used reasoning effort none, and the other models used temperature zero without reasoning mode. No saved response reports reasoning tokens or traces. Local runs of the main bank took 1.54 device-hours, and its API responses cost about US$4. We match models to released BFCL V4 scores (Patil et al., 2025) from the public 16 December 2025 function-calling snapshot, without rerunning BFCL, reporting Overall, Multi-Turn, and Agentic in parallel.

sections.title: 4 Results
sections.content: Core accuracy was lower than single-step arithmetic accuracy for every model, 31.7% versus 84.9% pooled (Figure 3a). All models remain in the analyses, including low-scoring and frequently truncated ones  (Table 2)  . Larger models scored higher in five of six adjacent-size core comparisons within Granite, Llama, and Falcon, and tied in one. Generation differences in Granite and Llama prevent isolating parameter count.

sections.title: Intermediate states and multiple targets
sections.content: Intermediate-state queries test end-state shortcuts by asking for earlier values (Figure 4a). Twenty trajectories, each with five entities, contain nine slots, with three same-sign one-point updates to the queried entity, four updates to others, and two inactive slots. Each trajectory supplies one query after each target update, giving 60 items. Later states were not easier to report. Mean third-update accuracy was 23.3 points [10.6, 35.8] below firstupdate accuracy  (Table 3)  . Twenty trajectories yield 120 multi-target and readout items querying = 1, 2, or 4 entities (Figure 4b). Each target receives two noncancelling updates, plus four operations on unqueried entities, giving 6, 8, or 12 operations. Readout redirects target updates to other entities while preserving initial states, slot order, and operation signs and magnitudes. Queried values therefore equal their initial values. sections.title: 4.4 Sensitivity to the response protocol
sections.content: On 60 shared core items across 18 models, the larger budget added 195 correct responses under last-integer scoring, and the combined instruction added 400 more, reaching 950/1,080 (88.0%, Figure 3c, Table 5). The instruction change thus accounted for most of the gain. Under large budget, truncation disappeared but one-integer scoring still yielded 342 correct responses. Responses containing several integers received no credit. The user/system instruction variant increased pooled accuracy at the unchanged budget and scoring rule, with eleven models improving, two tying, and five declining  (Table 5)  . Because both instructions changed, the gain cannot be assigned to either alone. Written steps improved all 18 models. Bare-number answers numbered 813, 986, and 0 of 1,080 under the core, instruction, and written-steps protocols. Truncations numbered 217, 80, and 4. Relative to the core, the instruction variant had 123 wrong-to-correct gains and 35 losses, and written steps had 615 gains and 7 losses (Appendix F). Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5 scored 0/60 and 14/60 under the core protocol, truncating most responses. Both scored 60/60 under both largebudget and written-steps protocols with last-integer scoring  (Table 5)  . Low core accuracy alone therefore does not imply inability to solve the underlying state-tracking problems.

sections.title: 4.6 Association with BFCL
sections.content: Across all 18 models, core accuracy was positively associated with all three BFCL criteria (Kendalls τb from 0.417 to 0.449), with wide pointwise 95% intervals, all above zero  (Table 6)  . All paired Kendall differences, core minus arithmetic and core minus cancellation, had intervals including zero, so the association does not single out state tracking  (Table 6)  . Without the four models that truncated most core responses, core minus arithmetic became positive at 0.096, 0.005, and 0.098, with intervals still including zero. Leaving out one provider group at time moved these estimates but kept the cores association with BFCL Overall positive, with point estimates from 0.325 to 0.702. Removing Anthropic alone moved the core-minus-arithmetic difference for Overall from 0.267 to 0.011. With Pearson correlations of correct counts, core minus cancellation was 0.269 to 0.336 and all three intervals were above zero. The core minus arithmetic intervals still included zero (Table A3). Across the 15 BFCL subcategory scores, no core-minus-arithmetic or core-minuscancellation interval lay above zero, and the coreminus-arithmetic intervals for the non-live, live, and missing-function categories lay below zero. Protocol-specific BFCL associations are shown in Table 7. Instructions and Written steps had higher point estimates than Core, but their paired difference intervals included zero (Table A2).

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Core accuracy lagged arithmetic, and multi-target tracking lagged readout (Table 2, Figure 4). With the sequence visible, final answers cannot distinguish state maintenance from recomputation or establish equivalence to human span tasks. Changing instructions altered scores on identical items, with the combined instruction accounting for most of the protocols gain (Figure 3c). Low core accuracy is therefore not condition-invariant capacity estimate. Test conditions must accompany scores. Positive BFCL associations connect core performance to an external criterion, but uncertain differences from simpler tasks limit their interpretation  (Table 6)  . The probe is better used to locate answer degradation under reported conditions than as substitute for tool-use evaluation.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced WMIP to evaluate cumulative state tracking through programmable tasks, executable reference answers, and protocol comparisons on identical items. Across 18 LLMs, strong singlestep arithmetic performance did not ensure reliable cumulative tracking, and accuracy declined as update sequences grew. Positive associations with public BFCL scores further connected core performance to an external measure of tool-use performance. Changing the response protocol substantially altered accuracy on the same problems, with the combined instruction contributing more improvement than the larger output budget. Together, these findings show that measured tracking performance reflects both cumulative task demands and response conditions. By making these factors configurable and comparisons reproducible, WMIP 8 provides framework for investigating where statetracking accuracy degrades and how output conditions affect performance. Lee J. Cronbach and Paul E. Meehl. 1955. Construct validity in psychological tests. Psychological Bulletin, 52(4):281302.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: The visible sequence and final answers cannot distinguish state maintenance from recomputation or establish equivalence to human working-memory tasks. Scores depend on instructions, formatting, and output limits. One-integer responses do not rule out written steps or hidden computation. Protocol changes are bundled, while depth and control comparisons also vary task content. The 18-model convenience panel limits generalization. Modelbootstrap intervals omit item-sampling uncertainty and provider dependence and are not adjusted for multiplicity. BFCL is the sole external criterion, based on historical snapshot with partly documented settings. We report associations without matched reruns, held-out predictive evaluation, or comparisons with published probes under their official protocols.

sections.title: A Task Generation and Prompts
sections.content: Core initial values are integers from 5 to 20. Gains draw from 1 to 10. Losses draw from 1 to 5 subject to leaving at least one point. Transfers draw from 1 to 3 subject to the giver retaining at least one point. The implementation substitutes one-point gain or no-transfer operation when the corresponding sampled update is unavailable. For core depth K, generation seed s, and probe index i, the random stream uses + 1000K + i. Each depth has four seed cells, each retaining five nondegenerate items. Replacement indices advance within the same cell. The item records in the supplementary material retain the original cell slot and replacement index. Section 3.1 gives one complete frozen core prompt. The instruction variant begins with Track the following point updates carefully., labels the final query Question:, and ends with Answer with ONLY the number. Section 3.2 gives its system message and the written-steps instruction. Both protocols link to the core items by source item identity, not by output order. The wording variants use separate seed bank of 30 instances, ten each at = 3, 5, 7. These items use gains and losses only and were not redrawn. In 7 of the 30, no update involves the queried entity, so the answer equals its initial value. All five 11 templates share each items initial values, updates, query, and reference answer. The minimal template appends Respond with ONLY the final number. The other four retain their numerical-answer instructions.

sections.title: B Scoring Specifications
sections.content: The numerical parser removes dollar signs and supported three-digit thousands separators, then extracts integer substrings matching the regular expression -?d+. The core rule requires exactly one match equal to gold, while the written-steps protocol uses the final match. The bare-number diagnostic additionally removes supported markdown markers and final period and requires the remaining string to be single integer. Scoring uses the complete recorded response, including one ending at the length limit. Parsers for the assignment items. Parser 1 removes complete <think> segments and lowercases the response, accepting gold as substring or as the normalized first word. Parser 2 removes asterisks/backticks, surrounding space, and final period, then requires exactly one distinct vocabulary member, found at word boundaries, equal to gold. Repetitions of that member and text outside the vocabulary can still pass. Parsers for the set and count items. For counts, Parser 1 removes complete <think> segments and accepts gold if it equals the first or last unsigned digit string, while Parser 2 uses the one-integer rule. For sets, Parser 1 lowercases, splits on commas, and deletes standalone no permissions or nothing. Empty-set gold also passes if the response contains no or nothing. Parser 2 normalizes markup, case, surrounding space, and final periods, splits on commas or the independent word and, and requires exact set equality. Only standalone no permissions, nothing, or none denotes an empty set. An empty response fails. Parser 2 does not delete <think> segments. Table A1 lists all seven disagreements. Five are incorrect or contradictory permission responses, one is spelling or word-boundary difference, and one is an empty-set response with redundant negative phrases.

sections.title: C Execution and Model Identity
sections.content: Local inference uses pinned weight and tokenizer revisions, vLLM 0.30.0 (Kwon et al., 2023), unquantized bfloat16, vendor chat templates, and temperature zero. Small models ran on 40 GB MIG instances of NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPUs. The mainbank Llama-3.3-70B run used two NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs with 96 GB each and tensor parallelism of two. OpenRouter API requests fix the original provider and disable fallback, and GPT-5.2 requests omit temperature. Saved responses pass identity and provider checks. Local repositories and frozen revisions are in the supplementary material, with technical reports for Granite 3.0 (IBM Granite Team, 2024), Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025). Vendorinserted dates are retained. The API models are GPT-5.2, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-mini, Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, Command (Team Cohere et al., 2025), and Command R7B. Exact request identifiers and model metadata are retained in the supplementary material. Preflight checks verify service identity and settings without selecting models by answer accuracy. BFCL criterion inputs and available parameter counts are in the supplementary material. Local execution used approximately 1.50 devicehours for the main bank, 0.34 for the intermediatestate and multi-target blocks, and 0.26 for the largebudget protocol, counting each MIG instance or full GPU as one device. These totals exclude hosted runs, failed/stopped jobs, separate tests, and the superseded multi-target runs (Appendix G). Returned usage reports sum to approximately US$4.032 for 6,720 main-bank responses and 40 successful preflight checks. Across all recorded October runs, including pilots, diagnostics, failed or stopped attempts, and superseded runs, allocations totalled 1.87 A100 MIG instance-hours and 1.84 RTX PRO 6000 GPU-hours. These resource units are reported separately. Returned API usage across these runs totalled US$5.642. Provider GPU-hours, unitemized retries, offline CPU work, and compute preceding these runs are unavailable. Analyses use NumPy 2.4.3 and SciPy 1.17.1. The supplementary README documents the released artifacts, analysis outputs, execution records, detailed timing, cost accounting, and BFCL sources and mappings. The synthetic tasks contain no personal data. Prompts and reference answers are in English, and the materials are intended for research evaluation of LLMs. Code uses the MIT License. Data, figures, and documentation use CC BY 4.0, and BFCL score files retain Apache-2.0 with source attribution. Granite and Qwen models use Apache 2.0,

On BIGBench Hards object-swap task, three 2022 models achieved between 53% and 85% accuracy with chain-of-thought prompting, up from near chance. Scores were averaged over three, five, and seven swaps (Suzgun et al., 2023). Other tasks apply up to ten swaps, where chain-of-thought prompting also raises accuracy (Rezaee et al., 2025). Chen et al. (2024) ask models to add list of integers without writing steps. They report that the strongest models directly output sums of more than ten addends and that accuracy falls as the number of addends increases. Their task keeps one running total, whereas our core items distribute updates across three entities. La Malfa et al. (2024) ask for one variables final value after short programs of additions, subtractions, and assignments. They note that most errors occurred when model output only the final result, not the execution trace. Programmable memory tests. Beyond quantity updates, Minerva includes set updates and composite state tracking. Its main quantity-state evaluation uses 200 operations, with an ablation over operation count (Xia et al., 2025).
